You build a clear argument: you present ideas in order, weigh up the arguments for and against, draw conclusions and express agreement or disagreement politely.

To put arguments in order: innanzitutto, in secondo luogo, inoltre, infine, in conclusione.
To weigh up two ideas: da un lato… dall'altro, è vero che… ma, certo… però.
To introduce an objection: tuttavia, eppure, invece, mentre.
To express cause and consequence: dato che, visto che, siccome; quindi, perciò, di conseguenza.
To express agreement or disagreement with nuance: sono d'accordo, non del tutto, non è detto che.
To step into a discussion politely: posso aggiungere una cosa?, mi lasci finire.
Florence, April, the evening before the meeting. Pietro has been given two minutes to speak. Bellini helps him prepare his speech at the kitchen table while Graziella washes the dishes.
Professor, I've written everything, but it's a disaster. I put things down as they came to me.
That's normal. A speech is like a restoration: first you put things in order. How do you begin?
Sincere, but weak. Try this: "First of all I'd like to thank everyone for coming." Then you present the problem.
But the lady from the company will say they paid for the building and can do what they like with it.
Then you agree with her, but only halfway. "It's true that the building is yours, but the neighbourhood belongs to everyone."
Nice! And then? I have three arguments: Grandma, the ribollita and Grandpa Aldo.
Then use the right words: "in the first place", "moreover", "finally". And at the end a clear conclusion: "consequently, we ask that…"
Can I add something? Put the ribollita last. Good things are saved for the end.
Grandma, I don't entirely agree. Grandpa is more important than the ribollita.
You're right. But Grandpa ate ribollita every day. So they're connected.
See? Your grandmother has just made a perfect argument. Complete with a "so".
"dare ragione" = to agree with someone, to say they're right
Two double pairs, NN and TT: in-nan-zi-TOOT-to.
Double PP, "AU" as a diphthong: ap-PLOW-so.
innanzitutto, in primo luogo, prima di tutto
in secondo luogo, poi, inoltre, per di più
Infine, c’è la questione della memoria.
In conclusione, la trattoria deve restare.
"Inoltre" adds an argument in the same direction. "Per di più" is stronger: "what's more".
Da un lato il turismo porta lavoro, dall’altro svuota il quartiere.
È vero che il palazzo è vostro, ma il quartiere è di tutti.
Certo, la società deve guadagnare; però non a ogni costo.
Non solo la trattoria, ma anche la libreria ha chiuso.
"È vero che… ma" is the most elegant form of disagreement: first you acknowledge the other person's partial truth, then you make your point.
Il turismo cresce, eppure i negozi chiudono.
Io pago 1100 euro; i turisti, invece, pagano a notte.
Lui guadagna, mentre noi ce ne andiamo.
"Mentre" can also mean "while" in a time sense (Mentre cucinavo…). In argument it means contrast: "whereas".
dato che / visto che (at the start of the sentence)
Example: «Dato che gli affitti sono raddoppiati, molte famiglie se ne vanno. Di conseguenza, il quartiere si svuota.»
"Siccome" always comes at the start of the clause: "Siccome piove, resto a casa". NOT: "Resto a casa siccome piove" (then you use "perché").
Non è detto che sia così.
Condivido il suo punto di vista.
Su questo punto la penso diversamente.
"Non è detto che" takes the congiuntivo: "Non è detto che i turisti portino ricchezza" = It's not certain that tourists bring wealth.

The meeting had been called for six o'clock on a Thursday in April, but by half past five the trattoria was already full. Marco had pushed the tables against the walls and lined up all the chairs in the place, plus thirty folding chairs lent by the parish of Santo Spirito. It wasn't enough. People sat on the windowsills, on the counter, even on the steps of the staircase leading to the flat upstairs. Outside, on the pavement of Via Maggio, those who hadn't managed to get in listened through the open window.

Everyone was there. Signor Franco in the front row, wearing his special-occasion tie. Davide's mother, just off her night shift, with tired eyes. The newsagent, the baker, the fruit seller, the barman. Don Lorenzo, who had asked to say a prayer and to whom Graziella had replied: "Afterwards, Father. First we discuss, then we pray." Chiara and Matei stood near the kitchen door. Giulia was holding Viola, who had decided to take part in the meeting by banging a wooden spoon on the table.

At a table set crosswise in front of everyone sat three people. In the middle, Sandro Mancini, acting as moderator. On the right, the city's councillor for culture, Paola Neri, an elegant lady with a red notebook. On the left, the Arno Living representative, Ms Valeria Conti: thirty-five, a blue suit, a folder full of documents and the air of someone who knows that tonight she will be the least loved person in the room. Davide, sitting on the floor in a corner, had already started drawing her.

Mancini opened the meeting by explaining the rules: three minutes each, no insults, and anyone who wants to speak raises their hand. Then he gave the floor to Ms Conti. She stood up, thanked everyone in a calm voice and began. "First of all I'd like to say that I understand your concern. However, I must also explain our point of view. The building needs two million euros of work: the roof, the stairs, the electrical system. The Lenzi heirs couldn't pay for it. Consequently, without us the building would have fallen to pieces."

"We are a company, not a charity," she went on. "We have to recover what we've spent. It's true that short-term rentals earn more than ordinary rents, but it's also true that they bring jobs: cleaning, maintenance, restaurants." Someone at the back whistled. Mancini raised a hand. Ms Conti finished without losing her composure: "Finally, I want to make one thing clear: nobody has signed anything yet. I'm here to listen." She sat down. A cold silence filled the trattoria.

The first hand raised was that of Davide's mother, Rita. She spoke softly, without looking at anyone. "I'm a night nurse at Santa Maria Nuova hospital. When I came to San Frediano fifteen years ago, I paid five hundred euros in rent. Now I pay eleven hundred. My landlord has already told me that next year he wants to rent to tourists. Since I can't pay more, I'll have to leave. But if we all leave, who will look after the tourists when they fall ill?"

The first applause of the evening was for her. Then a young man nobody expected raised his hand: Lorenzo, twenty-eight, the baker's grandson. "Sorry, I'd like to say something different," he began, a little red in the face. "On the one hand I understand Rita, and I'm sorry. On the other, I rent two flats to tourists, and thanks to them I've stayed in Florence. Without short-term rentals I'd have had to go and work in London, like all my friends. It's not certain that tourism is always the enemy."

There were murmurs, a few protests. But Signor Franco, surprisingly, raised his hand to answer him kindly. "You're right, Lorenzo, and you did well to say it. The problem isn't you, with your two flats. The problem is when tourists outnumber residents. I was a stationmaster for thirty-five years. A station where everyone arrives and nobody lives is a station. A neighbourhood where everyone arrives and nobody lives… is still a station."

Then it was Pietro's turn. He stood up on his chair, because otherwise nobody at the back could see him, and read the sheet he had prepared with Bellini. "First of all I'd like to thank everyone for coming. It's true that the building belongs to the company, but the neighbourhood belongs to everyone. I have three arguments. In the first place, my grandmother has worked here since she was fifteen. Moreover, it was here that my grandfather Aldo ate ribollita every day for a year before he had the courage to ask her to the cinema. If the trattoria closes, that story will no longer have a place."

"Finally," said Pietro, looking at his grandmother, "there's the ribollita. Grandma says good things are saved for the end. Grandma's ribollita is the best in Florence. Grandpa said so, Professor Bellini says so, and now I say so too. Consequently, we ask that the trattoria stay where it is. Thank you." He climbed down from the chair amid applause so loud that Viola, frightened, stopped banging her spoon. Ms Conti wasn't clapping, but Davide, from his corner, noticed that she had taken off her glasses and was cleaning them very carefully.

The last to speak was Bellini. He rose slowly, his hands behind his back, as when he explained a painting to students. "In November 1966," he began, "when the Arno came into this trattoria and into the churches of the whole neighbourhood, my grandfather Ernesto worked for weeks in the mud. It wasn't the tourists who helped him. It was young men like Aldo, the families of San Frediano, the baker, the cobbler, Mrs Lenzi, who brought coffee to the volunteers. A city isn't made of buildings. It's made of people who, when the water comes, stay."

"I have been restoring paintings for forty years," he went on. "And I can assure you of one thing: a beautiful painting, if you take away its face, is worth nothing any more. Of course, the frame remains. The colours remain. But nobody stops to look at it any more. Well, a neighbourhood without residents is a painting without a face. Ms Conti, you can restore the roof, the stairs, the electrical system. However, if you send the people away, you will have restored an empty frame." He sat down. This time nobody applauded at once. There was a long silence, the kind that is worth more than applause.

It was Councillor Neri who broke it. She opened her red notebook and read what she had written during the evening. "I've heard many arguments, and almost all of them fair," she said. "On the one hand, the city cannot stop a private party from selling or buying a building. On the other, there is a register of the city's historic shops: premises on it are protected and cannot change their business. A trattoria open since 1952, with the same family and the same recipe, meets all the requirements. We will start the application tomorrow."

This time the applause made the glasses on the shelves shake. Signor Franco blew his nose into his special-occasion tie. Rita hugged Davide, who didn't stop drawing. Lorenzo, the baker's grandson, went to shake Pietro's hand: "Good speech. You almost convinced me." "Almost?" asked Pietro. "Almost is already a lot," answered Lorenzo, laughing. "My grandfather says that in Florence nobody is ever completely convinced."

Mancini declared the meeting closed. It was then that Graziella, who hadn't said a word all evening, came out of the kitchen with an enormous pot. "I can't make speeches," she said. "I can make ribollita. Anyone who spoke has the right to a plate. Anyone who didn't, too." She began serving everyone, one by one. When she reached Ms Conti, who was putting her documents back in her folder, she stopped for a moment. Then she filled her plate to the brim. "You too," she said. "Especially you."

Ms Conti hesitated, then sat down and ate. She ate slowly, in silence, while around her the trattoria filled with voices again. When she had finished, she stood up, carried her plate into the kitchen herself and said something quietly to Graziella that nobody heard. Graziella looked at her in surprise and nodded. Then Ms Conti said goodbye to everyone with a nod and went out into Via Maggio, where it was already dark.

"What did she tell you?" Pietro asked his grandmother as soon as the door had closed again. Graziella wiped her hands on her apron. "She told me her grandmother also had a trattoria, in Prato. That she closed it in 2003 because the landlord had doubled the rent. And that her ribollita was almost as good as mine." She paused. "Almost," she repeated, and for the first time in a month she smiled. "Lorenzo is right. Almost is already a lot."

That night Davide finished the portrait of Ms Conti. He hadn't drawn her as the villain of the story, with horns or a sneer, as someone had laughingly suggested. He had drawn her sitting alone at a table, with a plate of ribollita in front of her and her glasses in her hand, looking out of the window. Underneath he had written, in his crooked handwriting: "On the one hand… on the other." The following Saturday Bellini saw it hanging in the workshop and stood looking at it for a long time. "This boy," he said at last, "has understood argument better than all of us."
